questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: What Makes the Membrane Fluid
questions.stem: While fixing a common mistake, a student claims membrane fluidity depends only on temperature.

options.text: Fluidity also depends on lipid composition and cholesterol.
Temperature is the only factor affecting fluidity.
Fluidity is fixed and never changes.
Only proteins determine fluidity.

questions.explanation: Membrane fluidity is modulated by temperature, fatty acid saturation, chain length, and cholesterol. Temperature alone is insufficient.

questions.topic: Physiology: What Selectively Permeable Adds
questions.stem: While fixing a common mistake, a student thinks selectively permeable means completely impermeable.

options.text: Selectively permeable blocks all molecules.
Selectively permeable allows some molecules through while blocking others.
Selectively permeable lets everything pass freely.
Selectively permeable only blocks water.

questions.explanation: Selective permeability means differential passage, not total block or free passage. Water is often among the permeable molecules.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Net and Gross Movement at Equilibrium
questions.stem: While fixing a common mistake, a student says no molecules move at equilibrium.

options.text: Only net movement occurs at equilibrium.
All movement stops at equilibrium.
Gross movement continues; net movement is zero.
Equilibrium means molecules disappear.

questions.explanation: At equilibrium, molecules still move in both directions, but net movement is zero. Movement does not stop or vanish.

questions.topic: Physiology: Osmosis Is Defined by Its Solvent
questions.stem: While fixing a common mistake, a student defines osmosis as solute movement.

options.text: Osmosis occurs only in animal cells.
Osmosis is the movement of solute across a membrane.
Osmosis requires active transport of water.
Osmosis is the net movement of solvent across a semipermeable membrane.

questions.explanation: Osmosis refers to solvent, usually water, moving across a semipermeable membrane. It is passive and occurs in all cells.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: What a Carrier Contributes
questions.stem: While fixing a common mistake, a student thinks carrier proteins create pores.

options.text: Carrier proteins form permanent pores like channels.
Carrier proteins bind and transport specific molecules by changing shape.
Carrier proteins digest transported molecules.
Carrier proteins only transport water.

questions.explanation: Carrier proteins bind specific molecules and undergo conformational change to transport them. They are not pores, enzymes, or water-specific.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: What Active Transport Buys
questions.learningObjective: Explain energy cost of active transport
questions.stem: While fixing a common mistake, a student asks what active transport achieves with ATP.

options.text: It breaks molecules into smaller parts.
It moves molecules down their gradient faster.
It moves molecules against their concentration gradient.
It creates a membrane from scratch.

questions.explanation: Active transport uses ATP to move substances against their gradient. It is not merely faster diffusion, digestion, or membrane synthesis.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Two Conditions for a Membrane Potential
questions.stem: While fixing a common mistake, a student lists only ion concentration differences as needed for a membrane potential.

options.text: Neither is needed; potentials arise spontaneously.
Only concentration gradients are needed.
Only selective permeability is needed.
Both concentration gradients and selective permeability are needed.

questions.explanation: A membrane potential requires both a concentration gradient and selective permeability to ions. Neither alone suffices, and potentials do not arise spontaneously.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Why Resting Potential Sits Near the Potassium Balance
questions.learningObjective: Explain resting potential near K+ equilibrium
questions.stem: While fixing a common mistake, a student asks why resting potential is close to potassium equilibrium.

options.text: Sodium permeability dominates at rest.
The membrane is most permeable to potassium at rest.
Potassium is absent from the cell.
The sodium-potassium pump sets the potential alone.

questions.explanation: At rest, high potassium permeability pulls the membrane potential toward the potassium equilibrium. Sodium permeability is low, and the pump maintains gradients but permeability shapes the potential.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: The Threshold Potential
questions.stem: While fixing a common mistake, a student thinks any small depolarisation triggers an action potential.

options.text: Hyperpolarisation triggers an action potential.
Any depolarisation, however small, triggers an action potential.
Only depolarisation reaching threshold triggers an action potential.
Action potentials occur without any stimulus.

questions.explanation: An action potential requires depolarisation to reach threshold; subthreshold stimuli do not trigger it. Hyperpolarisation moves away from threshold.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Releasing Transmitter at a Nerve Ending
questions.stem: While fixing a common mistake, a student thinks neurotransmitters diffuse out continuously.

options.text: Neurotransmitters are made in the synaptic cleft.
Neurotransmitters leak out continuously without a signal.
Sodium directly releases vesicles without calcium.
Calcium influx triggers vesicle fusion and release.

questions.explanation: An action potential opens calcium channels; calcium triggers vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release. It is not continuous leakage or sodium-driven.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Ending a Neurotransmitter's Action
questions.stem: While fixing a common mistake, a student asks how a neurotransmitter's effect ends.

options.text: It remains bound forever.
Reuptake, enzymatic degradation, or diffusion clears it.
It is converted into an action potential.
It destroys the postsynaptic membrane.

questions.explanation: Neurotransmitter action ends by reuptake, enzymatic breakdown, or diffusion away. It does not remain bound, become an action potential, or damage membranes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Excitatory and Inhibitory Postsynaptic Potentials
questions.stem: While fixing a common mistake, a student thinks all postsynaptic potentials are excitatory.

options.text: IPSPs always trigger action potentials.
All postsynaptic potentials are excitatory.
IPSPs hyperpolarise or stabilise, reducing firing probability.
EPSPs always prevent firing.

questions.explanation: IPSPs make the membrane more negative or stable, lowering firing probability, whereas EPSPs depolarise and raise it. Not all potentials are excitatory.

options.text: Weak inputs never contribute to firing.
A single weak input always triggers an action potential.
Weak inputs are amplified by the synapse automatically.
Spatial or temporal summation combines inputs to reach threshold.

questions.explanation: Multiple weak inputs can sum spatially or temporally to reach threshold. A single weak input is usually subthreshold.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: The One-to-One Nerve to Muscle Relationship
questions.stem: While fixing a common mistake, a student thinks one nerve impulse may fail to trigger muscle contraction.

options.text: Nerve impulses never trigger muscle contraction.
At the neuromuscular junction, one impulse normally triggers one contraction.
Multiple impulses are always required for one contraction.
Muscle contraction occurs without nerve input.

questions.explanation: The neuromuscular junction is a reliable one-to-one synapse: one nerve impulse normally yields one muscle action potential and contraction. It is not summation-dependent or nerve-independent.

Hormones act only across synapses.
Hormones travel via blood to distant targets; neurotransmitters act across synapses.
There is no difference between them.

questions.explanation: Hormones are blood-borne signals to distant cells, whereas neurotransmitters act locally across synapses. They are not interchangeable.

questions.topic: Physiology: Why Only Some Cells Answer a Hormone

options.text: Non-target cells lack a nucleus.
All cells respond equally to every hormone.
Hormones are destroyed before reaching non-target cells.
Only target cells possess the matching receptor.

questions.explanation: Hormone action requires specific receptors; cells without the receptor do not respond. All cells do not respond, and degradation or nucleus absence is not the reason.

Negative feedback counteracts the change to restore set point.
Negative feedback ignores the change.
Negative feedback only works in plants.

questions.explanation: Negative feedback opposes the deviation and restores the set point. It does not amplify, ignore, or plant-limit the response.

questions.topic: Physiology: Why a Positive Feedback Loop Is Useful

options.text: It is never useful in physiology.
It maintains a stable set point continuously.
It drives a process to completion, such as childbirth.
It only occurs in disease states.

questions.explanation: Positive feedback amplifies a change to drive a process to completion, as in childbirth or blood clotting. It does not maintain stability or occur only in disease.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Evaporative Cooling in Thermoregulation
questions.stem: While fixing a common mistake, a student asks how sweating cools the body.

options.text: Cooling occurs without any heat transfer.
Sweat warms the skin by adding heat.
Sweat blocks heat loss entirely.
Evaporation of sweat removes heat from the skin.

questions.explanation: Sweat evaporation absorbs latent heat from the skin, cooling the body. It does not warm, block heat loss, or occur without heat transfer.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Why the Vasa Recta Is a Hairpin

options.text: It increases blood pressure in the kidney.
It preserves the medullary osmotic gradient via countercurrent exchange.
It filters blood cells from plasma.
It pumps water into the urine.

questions.explanation: The hairpin vasa recta acts as a countercurrent exchanger, preserving the medullary gradient while removing reabsorbed water and solutes. It does not raise pressure, filter cells, or pump water.

questions.topic: Physiology: What Drives Filtration at the Glomerulus

Active transport pushes fluid into Bowman's capsule.
Hydrostatic blood pressure drives filtration.
Diffusion of solutes drives water filtration.

questions.explanation: Glomerular filtration is driven by hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries. It is not active transport, pure osmosis, or solute diffusion.

The stomach absorbs most nutrients.
The large intestine absorbs all nutrients.
The small intestine is the main absorption site.

questions.explanation: The small intestine, with its villi and microvilli, is the primary site of nutrient absorption. The stomach and oesophagus have limited roles.

questions.topic: Physiology: Why a Lining Is Folded at Three Scales

They massively increase surface area for absorption.
They store digestive enzymes.
They pump blood through the gut.

questions.explanation: Folds, villi, and microvilli multiply absorptive surface area. They do not decrease area, store enzymes, or pump blood.

Independent binding of oxygen to haemoglobin.
Cooperative binding of oxygen to haemoglobin.
Oxygen is converted to carbon dioxide.

questions.explanation: Cooperative binding produces the sigmoidal curve, enabling efficient loading and unloading. Independent or random binding would be hyperbolic.

The osmotic gradient in the renal medulla.
The number of nephrons.
The pH of the blood.

Low pH reduces haemoglobin's oxygen affinity.
Low pH converts oxygen to carbon dioxide.

Action potentials stop entirely.
Calcium is no longer needed for release.

questions.explanation: Blocking calcium channels prevents the calcium influx that triggers vesicle fusion, greatly reducing release. Action potentials may still occur, and calcium remains required.

questions.topic: Physiology: Excitatory and Inhibitory Postsynaptic Potentials
questions.stem: While fixing a common mistake, a student asks what an IPSP does to membrane potential.

options.text: It always triggers an action potential.
It depolarises the membrane, increasing firing.
It has no effect on membrane potential.
It makes the membrane more negative or stable, reducing firing.

questions.explanation: An IPSP hyperpolarises or stabilises the membrane, making firing less likely. It does not depolarise or trigger action potentials.

questions.topic: Physiology: Summation of Many Weak Inputs
questions.stem: While fixing a common mistake, a student asks how temporal summation works.

options.text: Inputs from many sources sum at one instant.
Rapid repeated inputs from one source sum over time.
A single input is amplified by the synapse.
Temporal summation requires no repeated input.

questions.explanation: Temporal summation occurs when repeated inputs from one source arrive close in time and sum. Spatial summation involves many sources at once.

questions.stem: While fixing a common mistake, a student asks which signal can reach cells throughout the body.

A neurotransmitter released into a synapse.

questions.explanation: Hormones travel via blood to reach cells throughout the body. Neurotransmitters and action potentials act locally.
